# FY2025 Annual Safety Performance Report
### Board of Directors — Health, Safety & Environment

---

## 1. The board reading (what the year means in one paragraph)

**FY2025 is a year in which our injury outcomes improved and moved below the sector — while our exposure to a *serious* event rose and concentrated in two activities we already know are our most dangerous.** Lost-time and recordable rates both fell year-on-year and both now sit below the manufacturing benchmark. But high-potential incidents rose 22%, and they cluster in unprotected/improvised **work at height** and **contractor-managed lifting and mobile plant** — the same activities where a near-miss cluster appeared, and where several events had a *realistic worst-credible outcome of a fatality* despite minor actual harm. **The lagging numbers are good; they are also the most dangerous kind of good, because they can manufacture false assurance in the exact year our fatality exposure grew.** The single decision this paper puts to the Board is whether to **fund the FY2026 work-at-height assurance and contractor-safety uplift programme** — the pre-emptive control investment the exposure signal is calling for.

---

## 2. Headline reading — the divergence that matters

Two lines moved in opposite directions this year, and the gap between them is the story:

- **Outcomes (what already happened) got better.** LTIFR fell ~26% (from 6.00 to 4.44) and now sits ~18% below the sector benchmark; TRIR fell ~10% (2.31 → 2.07) and sits ~23% below sector. On a lagging-only view, FY2025 looks like a strong year.
- **Exposure (what is being set up to happen) got worse.** High-potential incidents rose 22% (50 → 61) and concentrated in work at height and contractor lifting — precisely the high-energy activities most correlated with fatal outcomes.

A board that reads only Section 4 (the outcome rates) would conclude the safety system is de-risking. A board that reads Section 6 (the HiPo/SIF lens) sees that **we reduced the frequency of the injuries we're used to while increasing the number of near-misses that could have been fatalities.** The correct governance response is *not* comfort — it is targeted investment in the two activities the precursor data has named for us.

---

## 3. Why leadership should not take assurance from the falling rates alone

Three cautions the Board should hold alongside the improvement:

1. **Small-number volatility.** Six lost-time cases across 1.35 million hours is a small absolute base; a single case moves LTIFR by roughly 0.74. A 26% year-on-year improvement is real and welcome, but it rests on a handful of events and should not yet be read as a durable, structural trend — one bad quarter would erase it.
2. **The lagging rate is silent on severity potential.** TRIR/LTIFR count what *did* happen, not what *nearly* did. Our worst near-misses this year carried fatal worst-credible outcomes and are invisible in Section 4. Managing to the lagging rate alone would steer investment away from exactly where the fatal risk sits.
3. **Part of the HiPo rise is better seeing, not only more danger — but that does not neutralise it.** Near-miss reporting is up 30% and leadership safety tours up 33%; a maturing reporting culture surfaces more high-potential events, so some of the +22% reflects improved detection. That is a *good* signal for culture. It does **not** explain away the *concentration* of those events in work at height and contractor lifting — better reporting tells us where to look, and it is pointing at our two highest-energy activities.

## 4. Lagging indicators — outcomes (with readings)

Rates computed deterministically on OSHA-standard bases (recordable/DART ×200,000 hours; LTIFR ×1,000,000 hours) from 14 recordable, 9 DART, and 6 lost-time cases over 1,350,000 hours worked.

| Indicator | FY2025 | FY2024 | Year-on-year | Sector benchmark¹ | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TRIR** | **2.07** | 2.31 | ▼ ~10% | 2.7 | Below sector by ~23%; a genuine improvement on a stable-to-lower recordable count. |
| **DART** | **1.33** | [GAP]² | [GAP]² | [GAP]³ | ~64% of recordables reached days-away/restricted/transfer — a high severity ratio worth watching; no prior-year DART or sector DART supplied to trend it. |
| **LTIFR** | **4.44** | 6.00 | ▼ ~26% | 5.4 | Fell ~26% year-on-year *and* sits ~18% below the sector benchmark — the strongest lagging result in the paper, tempered by the small-number and severity-potential cautions in §3. |

¹ Sector benchmarks: manufacturing, **BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII), 2023** (user-supplied). See §9 for the benchmark-vintage caveat.
² FY2024 DART not supplied → year-on-year DART trend is a **[GAP]**; not estimated.
³ No sector DART benchmark supplied → **[GAP]**; not invented.

**So what:** the outcome side of the ledger is favourable and defensibly below sector — but note the elevated DART share (9 of 14 recordables), which says that when we *are* hurt, the injuries are consequential, not trivial.

## 5. Leading indicators — what shapes the next outcome (with readings)

These are the predictive, controllable measures. They are broadly improving, with two that the exposure picture makes material.

| Indicator | FY2025 | Target | vs FY2024 | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Training completion | 94% | 95% | ▲ +6 pts (from 88%) | Strong recovery, marginally (1 pt) short of target — close the gap, don't celebrate it. |
| **Audit / inspection closure** | **81%** | **90%** | ▲ +8 pts (from 73%) | Improving but **9 points short of target** — the most material leading gap. Open audit findings in a year of rising work-at-height/contractor exposure mean corrective actions may be sitting open in exactly the activities generating our HiPo events. This is an assurance-loop weakness, not a paperwork one. |
| Near-miss reporting rate | ▲ +30% YoY | — | ▲ | A maturing reporting culture — more hazards surfaced before they become injuries. Read as a positive, and as the reason we can see the HiPo concentration at all. |
| CAPA on-time closure | 86% | [GAP]⁴ | [GAP]⁴ | Reasonable, but 1 in 7 corrective actions closes late; late closure on a HiPo action is unmitigated exposure carried forward. No target or prior-year value supplied. |
| Leadership safety tours | 120 | — | ▲ +33% (from 90) | Visible-leadership commitment materially up — a credible driver of the reporting improvement. |

⁴ No target or FY2024 value supplied for CAPA on-time closure → **[GAP]**; trend not asserted.

**So what:** culture and engagement indicators (near-miss reporting, tours, training) are moving the right way. The one leading indicator that undercuts the story is **audit/inspection closure at 81%** — the mechanism by which we *close out* known hazards is lagging its target in the year our known hazards became more dangerous.

## 6. HiPo / SIF lens — the exposure reading (interpreted)

*This is the section a lagging-rate table hides, and the one the Board should weight most heavily.*

**High-potential (HiPo) incidents rose to 61, up 22% from 50.** They are not scattered — they concentrate in two activities:

- **Unprotected / improvised work at height**, and
- **Contractor-managed lifting and mobile-plant operations** (mirrored by the year's near-miss cluster in work-at-height and contractor mobile-plant work).

Several of these events had a **realistic worst-credible outcome of a fatality** despite minor actual harm. In serious-injury-and-fatality (SIF) terms, these are precursors: the conditions empirically correlated with life-altering outcomes were present, and only circumstance separated a near-miss from a funeral.

**What this reveals about where the next serious event is most likely.** The precursor data has effectively named our two highest-probability locations for the next fatality: a fall from height where edge protection was absent or improvised, or a person struck during a contractor lift or mobile-plant movement. These are not hypothetical — they are the aggregate signal of 61 real events this year. The organisation's fatal risk is now **concentrated and legible**, which is the precondition for controlling it before it materialises.

**The governance implication.** We are in the classic pre-event pattern: improving lagging metrics running *alongside* rising serious-incident potential in identifiable activities. Boards that miss the next fatality almost always had this exact divergence in front of them and read the falling injury rate as the whole picture. The correct response is to treat the HiPo concentration — not the LTIFR — as the leading edge of risk, and to resource controls at the top of the hierarchy (eliminate the need to work at height / design out the improvised access; engineer contractor lift exclusion zones and physical separation of people from mobile plant) rather than relying on procedure, supervision and PPE alone.

## 7. Material risks carried into FY2026

| Risk | Signal behind it | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Fall from height (fatal potential)** | HiPo concentration + near-miss cluster in unprotected/improvised work at height | Rising exposure |
| **Contractor lifting / mobile-plant strike (fatal potential)** | HiPo concentration + near-miss cluster in contractor mobile-plant ops | Rising exposure |
| **Assurance-closure lag** | Audit/inspection closure 81% vs 90% target; CAPA on-time 86% | Improving but below target |
| **Psychosocial risk** | Named strategic priority; **no leading/lagging metric supplied this period [GAP]** — currently unmeasured, therefore unmanaged | Unquantified |

## 8. Assurance & governance (how much confidence the data warrants)

- **Data basis.** Lagging rates are computed deterministically on fixed OSHA bases from the period's counts and hours — reproducible and defensible. Leading indicators are management-reported.
- **The assurance loop is the weak link.** With audit/inspection closure at 81% and CAPA on-time closure at 86%, the Board should note that a meaningful share of *identified* hazards is not yet *closed* — and closure lag concentrated in work-at-height/contractor findings would directly explain persistent HiPo exposure. Recommend the FY2026 management review (ISO 45001 cl. 9.3) track closure rate *by activity*, not just in aggregate.
- **Psychosocial blind spot.** A stated strategic priority with no measure attached is a governance gap: ISO 45003 provides the framework to baseline it. The Board is being asked to prioritise something we are not yet measuring.
- **This paper is decision-support.** It must be reviewed and owned by a competent person; it does not itself constitute sign-off, legal advice, or regulatory assurance.

---

## 9. Basis, benchmarks & limitations (defensibility)

- **Benchmark source & vintage.** Sector comparators are manufacturing figures from the **BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII), 2023** (user-supplied): TRIR 2.7, LTIFR 5.4. Our rates are FY2025; comparing FY2025 performance to a 2023 benchmark carries a ~2-year vintage mismatch — the sector position is directionally sound but should be refreshed against the latest SOII release before it is quoted externally.
- **Like-for-like bases.** TRIR/DART use the OSHA 200,000-hour base; LTIFR uses the 1,000,000-hour base; benchmark comparisons are on the same bases.
- **Data gaps carried, not filled:** FY2024 DART and sector DART (no DART trend or DART benchmark); CAPA on-time target and prior-year value; any quantified psychosocial measure. Each is flagged **[GAP]** above and none has been estimated.
- **De-identification & aggregation.** Inputs arrived de-identified and aggregated; all published categories exceed 5 individuals (14 recordable, 9 DART, 6 lost-time); no individual incident, injured person, or sub-5 cell is identifiable, and no re-identification key appears in this paper.

## 10. Decisions requested of the Board (ISO 45001 cl. 9.3 management-review outputs)

Governance-level asks — resource, policy, and accountability — not operational task lists.

| # | Decision the Board is asked to take | Recommended owner | Review / decision date |
|---|---|---|---|
| **D1** | **Approve FY2026 funding** for the combined **work-at-height assurance + contractor-safety uplift programme** — the pre-emptive control investment the HiPo/SIF concentration is calling for. This is the paper's primary ask. | Board / CEO (funding); HSE Director (programme) | By 31 July 2026 |
| **D2** | **Mandate top-of-hierarchy controls** for the two named activities (eliminate/engineer out improvised height access; physical exclusion & separation for contractor lifts and mobile plant) — set the policy expectation that PPE/procedure-only treatments are not acceptable for fatal-potential work. | Chief Operating Officer / Operations Director | Design agreed by 30 September 2026 |
| **D3** | **Set an accountable owner and target for contractor safety** as a standing governance line (pre-qualification, on-site control, and lift/mobile-plant management). | Head of Procurement / Contractor Management | Framework by 31 October 2026 |
| **D4** | **Require assurance-loop recovery**: audit/inspection closure back to ≥90%, tracked *by activity*, with work-at-height and contractor findings prioritised. | HSE Director | ≥90% by 31 December 2026 |
| **D5** | **Commission a psychosocial-risk baseline** (ISO 45003) so the stated priority becomes a measured, managed one from FY2026. | HR / People Director | Baseline by 31 December 2026 |

## 11. Outlook — FY2026 trajectory

- **Trajectory the indicators imply.** If the assurance loop is closed and top-of-hierarchy controls are funded for work at height and contractor lifting, the HiPo curve should bend down and the favourable lagging position should become *structural* rather than a single good year. Absent that investment, the most likely path is continuation of the current divergence — flat-to-improving lagging rates masking a serious event waiting on one of the two named activities.
- **Next-period focus:** (1) execute the D1 programme; (2) recover audit closure to target and track it by activity; (3) stand up the psychosocial baseline; (4) sustain the reporting-culture gains (near-miss +30%, tours +33%) that are giving us this visibility.
- **What the Board should ask to see next period:** HiPo count and *concentration* trend (not just LTIFR), audit-closure-by-activity, contractor-safety performance, and the first psychosocial baseline.
- **Emerging risk to watch:** psychosocial exposure — currently unmeasured, and therefore the risk most likely to surface without warning.
